docs.title: How the course runs
docs.text:
Two teaching modules with the ⚙ AI-assisted/agentic-SE practice thread woven through both, then a flexible end-of-term block:

  • Module 1 (Weeks 1–8). Foundations. Build a code language model: transformers, training, preferences, reasoning, RAG and agents, evaluation. Runs alongside Project 1 (build → use → evaluate & break → improve your own code LM).
  • Module 2 (Weeks 9–11): ML in Production. Requirements, architecture, quality assurance, operations, responsible engineering: for systems with LLM components.
  • Weeks 12–14. Midterm 2, advanced ⚙ topics from the current literature, then the Project 2 finish: draft → design presentations with preliminary results → final conference-format paper.

The full week-by-week schedule, grading, and policies are in the syllabus. Slide decks are posted on the slides page after each class.

docs.title: Reading List
docs.text:
A suggested reading list for this course, not a complete bibliography, and not everything the slides cite. It is mostly software engineering research, with the AI papers you need to make sense of it. Pick what your project needs.

For Project 2, your research abstract (due Fri, Oct 2) has to name the papers whose open question you are answering. Start from this page.

Venues and years are given for convenience; check the canonical version before you cite anything.

docs.title: Start here: where the field is going
docs.text:
• Hassan et al., Agentic Software Engineering: Foundational Pillars and a Research Roadmap, arXiv:2509.06216, the agenda the ⚙ thread follows; most sections end in an open question sized for a course project
  • Hassan et al., Towards AI-Native Software Engineering (SE 3.0), arXiv:2410.06107, the shorter vision paper
  • Fan et al., Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems, ICSE-FoSE 2023, the map of the whole area
  • Hou et al., Large Language Models for Software Engineering: A Systematic Literature Review, TOSEM 2024, the exhaustive version; use it to find work near your topic

docs.text:
• AI Teammates in SE 3.0: curated, continuously updated: https://github.com/SAILResearch/AI_Teammates_in_SE3
  • ICSE 2027 Competition Track: what the community thinks is worth competing on right now, and a possible venue for a strong artifact: https://conf.researchr.org/track/icse-2027/icse-2027-competition-track

docs.title: Code generation and how we evaluate it
docs.text:
• Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code, arXiv 2021. Codex, HumanEval, and the definition of pass@k
  • Liu et al., Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? (EvalPlus), NeurIPS 2023: weak tests inflate benchmark scores; the correction matters
  • Austin et al., Program Synthesis with Large Language Models (MBPP), arXiv 2021
  • Li et al., StarCoder: May the Source Be With You!, TMLR 2023, what an open, documented code-model release looks like
  • Joel, Wu & Fard, A Survey on LLM-based Code Generation for Low-Resource and Domain-Specific Programming Languages, TOSEM 2025: (instructor's work) where code LLMs stop working, and why
  • Wu & Fard, HumanEvalComm: Benchmarking the Communication Competence of Code Generation for LLMs and LLM Agent, TOSEM 2025, (instructor's work) what happens when the problem description is ambiguous, inconsistent or incomplete, and whether the model asks

docs.title: Agents for software engineering
docs.text:
• Jimenez et al., SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?, ICLR 2024, how agent progress is scored
  • Yang et al., SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering, NeurIPS 2024, the interface is the design
  • Wang et al., OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents, ICLR 2025, an open platform to experiment on

docs.title: AI-assisted development: the human evidence
docs.text:
• Peng et al., The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot, arXiv 2023, the controlled experiment everyone cites
  • Barke et al., Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models, OOPSLA 2023, acceleration vs. exploration; the best qualitative account
  • Vaithilingam et al., Expectation vs. Experience: Evaluating the Usability of Code Generation Tools, CHI EA 2022, people like the tools even when they do not help
  • Perry et al., Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, CCS 2023
  • Pearce et al., Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions, IEEE S&P 2022: the CWE-level security study; Project 2 topic B5 replicates its shape

docs.title: Testing, analysis and assurance
docs.text:
• Schäfer et al., An Empirical Evaluation of Using LLMs for Automated Unit Test Generation, TSE 2024
  • Lemieux et al., CODAMOSA: Escaping Coverage Plateaus in Test Generation with Pre-trained LLMs, ICSE 2023
  • Deng et al., Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Fuzzers (TitanFuzz), ISSTA 2023
  • Xia & Zhang, Keep the Conversation Going: Fixing 162 out of 337 Bugs for $0.42 Each Using ChatGPT, ISSTA 2024, repair as a conversation, with the cost reported
  • Wu et al., Investigating the Efficacy of Large Language Models for Code Clone Detection, ICPC ERA 2024: (instructor's work) an SE task LLMs are unexpectedly awkward at

docs.title: Engineering systems that contain a model
docs.text:
• Amershi et al., Software Engineering for Machine Learning: A Case Study, ICSE-SEIP 2019, the nine-stage workflow and what makes ML different
  • Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems, NeurIPS 2015: still the sharpest warning in the field
  • Wu, An Exploratory Study of V-Model in Building ML-Enabled Software: A Systems Engineering Perspective, CAIN 2024, (instructor's work) what a classical process model does and does not survive
  • Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting, FAT* 2019. Project 1's model card follows this
  • Gebru et al., Datasheets for Datasets, CACM 2021, and Project 1's data sheet follows this

docs.title: Doing empirical SE research well
docs.text:
• Ralph et al., ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standards for Software Engineering Research, read the standard matching your study type before writing the proposal; reviewers will
  • Wohlin et al., Experimentation in Software Engineering (Springer): the reference book for study design and threats to validity

docs.title: The AI side: enough to understand the above
docs.text:
• Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, NeurIPS 2017: the architecture
  • Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3), NeurIPS 2020: scale and in-context learning
  • Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla), NeurIPS 2022: why your Project 1 model gets ~20 tokens per parameter
  • Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, ICLR 2022
  • Ouyang et al., Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT), NeurIPS 2022
  • Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization, NeurIPS 2023: the simplification that stuck
  • Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models, NeurIPS 2022
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, NeurIPS 2020
  • Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, ICLR 2023, the loop every agent runs
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning, 2025

docs.title: How to find more
docs.text:
1. Chase citations. Take one paper above, read what it cites and what cites it (Google Scholar's "cited by"). Two hops usually reaches the frontier.
  2. Skim recent proceedings: ICSE, FSE, ASE, MSR, EASE, AIware. The last two years are enough for this course.
  3. Mine the lectures. Every lecture closes on open questions, and any slide making a specific claim shows its source at the foot.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Generative AI (and large language models (LLMs) in particular) is materially changing how software is built. This course examines that change from both directions: software engineering of generative AI systems (building, evaluating, and operating systems with learned components) and software engineering with generative AI (AI-assisted and agentic development workflows).

AI-assisted and agentic software engineering is not a standalone unit at the end, it is a thread that runs through the whole course. From Week 1, students use AI coding assistants and agents as their required development workflow (and learn to validate their output); the foundations module explains how those tools work by building one; the production module covers how to engineer, evaluate, and operate LLM-powered and agentic systems. The second half of the course runs as a research seminar: students (solo or in pairs) carry out an original research project and write it up as a conference-format paper, which is submitted to a suitable venue after the semester ends.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Probability and statistics, linear algebra, data structures
  • Programming maturity (Python); prior exposure to machine learning is helpful but not required
  • Graduate standing, or instructor permission for undergraduates

docs.title: Undergraduate students
docs.text:
This is a graduate course, and a small number of undergraduates take it with instructor permission. They do the same lectures, the same Project 1, and the same exams. Three adjustments are recommended: suggestions, not requirements, so that the graduate-level research expectations land more gently on a student who has not been taught them yet:

Recommended adjustment Project 2 pairing Project 2 is done solo or in pairs; undergraduates are encouraged to pair with a graduate student rather than working solo. Design presentation Undergraduates paired with a graduate student may co-present the design presentation rather than presenting alone.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

  1. Explain at a principled level how large language models are trained (pretraining, instruction tuning, RLHF/preference optimization) and how they generate output.
  2. Build, fine-tune, and evaluate a small code-generation language model end to end, including data preparation, tokenization, training, and benchmark evaluation.
  3. Analyze training datasets for provenance, bias, contamination, licensing, and governance implications.
  4. Explain embeddings as a representational framework and apply them to retrieval and similarity tasks (e.g., retrieval-augmented generation over codebases).
  5. Evaluate AI as a system component with defined cost, latency, reliability, safety, and privacy characteristics, and design systems that mitigate common failure modes (hallucination, adversarial inputs, miscalibration, prompt injection).
  6. Apply production ML practices (requirements, architecture, deployment, testing, monitoring, and MLOps) to systems with LLM components.
  7. Effectively use AI coding assistants and AI agents within a disciplined, collaborative development workflow (version control, code review, validation of AI-generated code), and design and evaluate agentic systems for SE tasks.
  8. Critically read and discuss current research in AI-assisted and agentic software engineering.
  9. Design and execute an empirical software engineering study involving generative AI, and communicate the results in a conference-quality research paper.

docs.title: Course Materials
docs.text: Two textbooks (no purchase is needed). The free materials listed below fully cover this course. T1 is a Manning book, but its companion repository (the complete, runnable code for every chapter) and the resources under it are enough on their own. If you want to support T1's author (Sebastian Raschka, a former UW–Madison professor), you are welcome to buy the book. T2 is freely readable online, and every other reading is a research paper available via arXiv or the ACM/IEEE digital libraries (through the MTU library).

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Component Weight Midterm exam 1 (Module 1) 10% Midterm exam 2 (Module 2) 10% Participation & in-class engagement 10% Project 1. Build and evaluate a small code language model 25% Project 2. Research project (conference submission) 45% Bonus: workshop submission (instructor-approved) +5%

There is no final exam. The two midterms are short, in-class exams: Midterm 1 covers the Module 1 foundations lectures taught through the Week 6 review (through reasoning: the Weeks 7–8 material on retrieval, agents and evaluation is not on it); Midterm 2 covers the Module 2 lectures. The ⚙ AI-assisted/agentic SE sessions are practice-oriented and are assessed through the projects, not an exam.

Bonus credit (+5% of the course grade). A team whose final paper is reviewed and approved by the instructor submits it to a suitable conference workshop or similar venue (e.g., an ICSE/FSE workshop, AIware, or an MSR/EASE track, chosen with the instructor over the winter break; the realistic deadlines fall January–March) and earns bonus credit for every team member. Target is a workshop paper of up to 8 pages (not including references). The bonus is awarded for a completed, instructor-approved submission: not for acceptance, which is decided long after grades are due. Approval means the paper meets a real venue's bar: a falsifiable research question, a fair baseline, reported variance, an honest threats-to-validity section, and compliance with the venue's formatting and AI-disclosure rules.

docs.title: Participation & in-class engagement (10%)
docs.text:
• Sign in Attendance is required for this course, please sign the sheet each class. We will apply a threshold such as 80% in the end so that one expects to get full marks with occasional exceptions (sick, occasional conflict, etc.)
  • Discussion is assumed: the paper discussions, the hands-on sessions and the design-presentation Q&A are how this class runs, and everyone is expected to join in naturally.
  • One way to lose points: disrespect. Every student's questions, answers and presentations are treated with respect. Dismissing or belittling another student's contribution costs participation credit.

docs.title: Project 1: Build and Evaluate a Small Code Language Model (25%, individual, Weeks 1–9)
docs.text:
Train a small code language model from scratch, use it on a real software engineering task, document how it fails, then make one evidence-based improvement and re-evaluate. Four phases with a recommended pace (Sep 25 / Oct 9 / Oct 16 / Oct 23); everything is due in one bundle on Fri, Oct 30. Full instructions, templates, compute guidance and the grading table: the Project 1 page on the course website.

A note on data. Anonymised Phase 3 findings may be used in a study of how this course is taught. Participation is voluntary, opt-in via a Week 1 consent form, and has no bearing on grades in either direction.

docs.title: Project 2: Research Project with Conference Submission (45%, solo or in pairs, Weeks 3–14)
docs.text:
Full spec: the Project 2 page (spec released soon) on the course website, with the proposal template (spec released soon), the suggested reading list, and the candidate venues.

An original research project on software engineering with/for generative AI, carried out solo or in pairs and written up as a conference-format paper. The goal is to take one question from idea to evidence to a paper an outside reviewer would take seriously, and then actually submit it. The rubric is the same for one student as for two; scope expectations scale with the number of hands, and the proposal is where scope is agreed. Undergraduates are encouraged to pair with a graduate student (see above: a suggestion, not a requirement).

The research thread starts in Week 3. Topics circulate on Fri, Sep 18, and by Fri, Oct 2 each student writes their paper's abstract, before doing the research: the context, the problem the literature leaves open (naming the papers), the proposed solution, and the claim they expect to defend, in 150–250 words. Writing it forces a context, a gap and a plan into one paragraph that either holds together or visibly does not: an evening's work in October instead of a lost month in November. Your Phase 3 findings table will later sharpen it (reread the abstract after red-teaming: several of the best questions come from there). Full-time execution begins Nov 2, giving five working weeks before the draft. Many projects extend the Project 1 experience directly: four of the circulated candidate topics reuse the class's own models, probes, and QA checks.

Feedback at every step. Every Project 2 deliverable (abstract, pitch, proposal, draft, presentation) comes back with feedback aimed at what to do next, while there is still time to act on it. Students are expected to take it seriously; they are also free to keep their own direction, provided they give the reason for setting a comment aside. Reasoned disagreement is how research works and is welcome here; quietly repeating the same weakness is not.

Why we submit to a real venue. Writing for an external audience is the pedagogy, not a trophy hunt. A real deadline and real reviewers force the things this course is about: a question you can actually answer, an honest baseline, results you can defend, and limitations you state yourself. Teams that make it that far learn more than any term paper could teach.

How submission works, and what the target is. The target venue is a conference workshop (ICSE/FSE workshops, AIware, MSR/EASE tracks and similar), on purpose: a workshop paper of up to 8 pages (not including references) is the right-sized ambition for one semester, and setting that expectation up front is healthier than chasing a top-tier main track. Papers are submission-ready on Dec 11; teams may post an arXiv preprint then. Over the winter break the instructor works with each team to pick the workshop whose scope and deadline fit their work: options are discussed in Week 12, and the deadlines that suit a December finish fall between January and March. Papers the instructor reviews and approves are submitted for +5% bonus credit (see Grading).

Grading is independent of the outcome. Your grade reflects the quality of the research and the writing: the study you designed, the evidence you gathered, the honesty of your analysis. Acceptance decisions arrive months after grades are final and play no part in them. A rigorous negative result earns full marks.

Milestones (weights are of the Project 2 grade):

Date Milestone Weight Fri, Sep 18 Topics circulated (posted on the course website): the research thread opens — Fri, Oct 2 Research abstract: context, gap, proposed solution, expected claim (150–250 words) 5 Mon, Oct 26 Five-minute topic pitch, in class 5 Fri, Oct 30 Written proposal (problem, method, baseline, evaluation plan): topic pivots allowed until Fri, Nov 20 15 Nov 2 – Dec 4 Execution: five working weeks; the ⚙ advanced sessions run alongside; check-ins in office hours — Fri, Dec 4 Full paper draft 15 Dec 7 / Dec 9 Design presentation + preliminary results 15 Fri, Dec 11 Final paper + artifact, submission-ready 45 after Instructor review over break → workshop chosen with each team; approved papers submitted +5% course bonus

docs.title: Use of AI tools
docs.text:
AI assistants (Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT, agents, etc.) are permitted, subject to the conditions below.

Conditions, in all cases:

  • You are accountable for everything you submit. AI-generated code and text must be reviewed, tested, and understood well enough that you can defend every line without the tool in the room. "The AI wrote it" is not a defence for work that is plagiarised, incorrect, insecure, or fabricated, including invented citations, which are treated as fabrication.
  • Disclose AI use in every deliverable: which tools, for what, and how you validated the output. Undisclosed use is an academic-integrity matter, not a style preference. It is also required to share the chat history of you and the AI.
  • Not permitted during the two in-person midterm exams.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text: Email (jie.jw.wu@mtu.edu) is answered within one business day on weekdays. If you have heard nothing in 48 hours, send a polite nudge: the message got buried, not ignored. Questions that need more than a few lines belong in office hours (Mon/Wed 9:30-10:30, Rekhi 207, by appointment). Announcements are made in class and on the course website; the website version is authoritative.

docs.title: Late work
docs.text: Project milestones lose 10% per day late (max 3 days) unless arranged in advance. The Dec 4 draft and Dec 11 final deadlines are firm because the presentation sessions and the submission timeline depend on them.

docs.title: Academic integrity
docs.text: All work is governed by the MTU Academic Integrity Policy. Collaboration within teams is expected; representing others' (or undisclosed AI) work as your own analysis is not.

docs.title: Accessibility and wellbeing
docs.text: MTU complies with the ADA and Section 504. Students with disabilities should contact Student Accessibility Services and the instructor early in the semester. docs.title: Project 1: Build and Evaluate a Small Code Language Model
docs.text: CS 5090 · Software Engineering with Generative AI Individual Project · 25% of Course Grade · Due Friday, October 30

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
In this project, you will train a small code language model from scratch, use it on a software engineering task, study how it fails, and make one evidence-based improvement. The goal is not to build a strong production model. The model is intentionally small so that you can understand the full workflow and inspect its behavior.

The project has four phases:

Phase Recommended pace Main task Deliverable 1. Build & understand by Sep 25 Train a small code LM and run one ablation Model card, data sheet, repository 2. Use by Oct 9 Use your model on 20 real SE inputs Task report 3. Evaluate & break by Oct 16 Design probes and document 10+ distinct failures Findings table (CSV) 4. Improve & re-evaluate by Oct 23 Make one change and re-run the same probes Improvement report, demo video

All components are submitted together on Friday, October 30. The intermediate dates are recommended milestones, not separate deadlines.

docs.title: What to submit
docs.text:
• Model card and data sheet
  • Code repository with reproducible training/configuration files
  • Phase 2 task report
  • Phase 3 findings table (CSV)
  • Phase 4 improvement report
  • 3-minute demo video
  • AI-use log
  • One-page handwritten AI-literacy reflection

docs.title: 2. Phase 1: Build & Understand
docs.text: Train a small GPT-style model from scratch. You may use either nanoGPT (recommended) or llama2.c. Find your own Python corpus: for example, a few permissively licensed repositories whose code you know or can judge. Different corpora across the class make the results more diverse and more interesting to compare. Keep collection light (a few hours, not a project of its own), and document in your data sheet how the data was filtered, deduplicated, tokenized, and split.

docs.title: Example model configuration
docs.text:
The following is one reasonable configuration for this project. You may adjust these settings based on your codebase, compute environment, or experimental goals. Document any major changes in your model card.

Setting Value Layers / heads / embedding size 6 / 6 / 384 Context length 512 tokens Tokenizer BPE, vocabulary 8,192; train only on the training split Training tokens approximately 20 × parameter count Precision bf16 when supported

docs.title: Recommended ablation options
docs.text:
After the baseline model trains, choose one ablation. The options below are recommended; you may propose a comparable alternative with instructor approval. Write down your prediction before running it, then retrain and compare final validation loss and one side-by-side generation sample.

Recommended option Question it helps you study Remove position embeddings Why does token order need to be represented? Use 1 attention head instead of 6 What is gained by multiple heads? Use 3 layers instead of 6 What is gained by depth? Remove LayerNorm How does normalization affect training stability? Context length 256 instead of 512 What does a longer context help with? Character-level tokenizer instead of BPE How does tokenization change training and generation?

docs.title: You should be able to explain
docs.text:
• How source code becomes tokens and why tokenizer choice matters.
  • How embeddings and self-attention provide contextual token representations.
  • What next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss optimize.
  • The difference between pre-training and inference.
  • How to interpret training and validation loss curves.
  • Why a small model trained on a small corpus produces fluent but incorrect code.

docs.title: Phase 1 deliverables
docs.text:
• Repository containing data preparation, training configuration, and instructions to reproduce the baseline and ablation runs.
  • Model card (Appendix A).
  • Data sheet (Appendix B).

If your training run fails after reasonable effort, contact the instructor about the spare checkpoint. You can still complete Phases 2–4, but you will not receive credit for missing Phase 1 work.

docs.title: 3. Phase 2: Use the Model on a Real SE Task
docs.text:
Use your own model on one software engineering task. Examples include code completion, docstring generation, test skeleton generation, or another task approved by the instructor. Use 20 real inputs from code that you understand well enough to judge.

For each input, classify the result as:

  • Accept as-is
  • Accept after editing
  • Reject

Keep three representative examples: your best result, your worst result, and one near-miss that initially looked correct but was not.

docs.title: Phase 2 deliverable
docs.text: Submit a 1–2 page task report using Appendix C. Report the three counts above and briefly explain what your model was useful for and when checking its output cost more time than writing the code yourself.

docs.title: 4. Phase 3: Evaluate & Break
docs.text:
Design a probe set that deliberately tests your model. Include ordinary inputs and cases that may expose weaknesses, such as misleading comments or names, long-context inputs, security-related prompts, or prompts similar to the training data.

Find at least 10 distinct failures. Record each failure in the findings table (Appendix D). Use the following category names exactly so results can be compared across the class.

Category Definition syntax Output does not parse invented-api Calls an API or function that does not exist wrong-logic Parses/runs but produces the wrong behavior insecure Introduces a security weakness memorised Reproduces training data nearly verbatim prompt-sensitive A small rewording changes the answer substantially context-ignored Ignores information clearly present in the input other Use only when none of the above applies; explain clearly

For every failure, include a specific one-line explanation of why it is wrong and whether a normal unit-test suite would likely catch it.

docs.title: 5. Phase 4: Improve & Re-evaluate
docs.text: Choose the failure category that appears most often in your Phase 3 findings. Form a hypothesis about its cause, make one change, and re-run the same probes.

docs.title: Possible intervention points
docs.text: Area Examples Data Remove unparseable files, improve deduplication, rebalance data Tokenizer Change vocabulary size or retrain on cleaner data Training More tokens, longer context, different learning-rate schedule Fine-tuning A small supervised fine-tuning pass on relevant examples Decoding Adjust temperature/top-p or sample multiple candidates

docs.title: Experimental rules
docs.text:
• State your hypothesis before running the experiment.
  • Change one thing only.
  • Re-run the same Phase 3 probes with the same decoding settings.
  • Report both improvements and regressions.
  • Report compute cost and validation loss when applicable.
  • A negative result is acceptable if it is measured and reported clearly.

docs.title: Phase 4 deliverables
docs.text:
• A 2–3 page improvement report using Appendix E.
  • Updated code/configuration in your repository.
  • A 3-minute recorded demo showing one probe before and after the change, plus your main quantitative result.

docs.title: 6. AI-Use Log
docs.text: You may use an AI coding assistant while completing the project. Keep a short log of meaningful interactions: what you asked, what you accepted, what required correction, and how you verified the result. The goal is to document where AI was useful and where it created extra work or confusion. Use Appendix F.

docs.title: 7. Handwritten Reflection
docs.text: At the end of the project, complete the one-page reflection in Appendix G by hand, without an AI tool. Scan or photograph the page and include it in your submission. It is graded for completion, not for giving a particular answer.

docs.title: 8. Grading
docs.text:
Component Weight Full credit requires Build & understand 25% Baseline + ablation are reproducible; prediction recorded before ablation; model card and data sheet show understanding Use 15% 20 real inputs; honest accept/edit/reject counts; three representative examples Evaluate & break 25% 10+ distinct failures; correct categories; specific explanations; test-suite column completed Improve & re-evaluate 25% Clear hypothesis; one change; same probes re-run; regressions and cost reported AI-use log, reflection, engineering quality 10% Complete log and handwritten reflection; repository is reproducible and results are traceable

Model quality itself is not graded. A small model that produces poor code is still useful for this project if you analyze it carefully. Likewise, your Phase 4 change does not need to improve the model; a well-designed negative result can receive full credit.

docs.title: 9. Compute
docs.text:
A GPU is strongly recommended for Phase 1 training. Expect roughly 2–6 GPU-hours per successful run and plan for 2–3 runs across the project. Kaggle, Google Colab, or a local GPU are all acceptable. Save checkpoints regularly and log training loss so you can reproduce and analyze your runs later.

If an ACCESS classroom allocation becomes available, instructions will be posted separately. The project does not depend on ACCESS availability.

docs.title: Appendices: Submission Templates
docs.text: You may copy these sections into Markdown files in your repository and fill them in.

docs.title: Appendix A: Model Card
docs.text:
• Model details: architecture, parameters, context length, vocabulary, seed, codebase commit, repository commit.
  • Intended use: course project / teaching artifact; not for unreviewed production code.
  • Training data: source, licenses, token count, deduplication, split strategy (refer to the data sheet for details).
  • Evaluation: validation loss, syntactic-validity rate, any other benchmark, and decoding settings.
  • Ablation: exact change, prediction written before the run, baseline vs. ablation loss, one sample comparison, and what you learned.
  • Limitations: measured failure modes, Python-only scope, memorization/contamination checks if performed.
  • Ethics/licensing/caveats: data licenses, secret/PII checks, and anything important that the headline metrics do not show.

docs.title: Appendix B: Data Sheet
docs.text:
• Motivation and source of the corpus.
  • Composition: file/token counts and licensing filters.
  • Collection: snapshot/commit and exclusions.
  • Preprocessing: cleaning steps, deduplication method and counts, tokenizer and vocabulary.
  • Splits: train/validation/test sizes; repository-level split; how leakage was checked.
  • Uses and limitations, including contamination risk.
  • Distribution: whether the data can be redistributed; if not, provide a reproducible recipe.

docs.title: Appendix C: Phase 2 Task Report
docs.text:
Length: 1–2 pages. Include your name, task, source of inputs, and why you can judge the outputs.

Outcome Count Accept as-is Accept after editing Reject
  • Define what "accept" means for your task.
  • Show three examples: best, worst, and near-miss.
  • What was the model actually useful for?
  • When did checking the model take more time than writing the code yourself?

docs.title: Appendix D: Findings Table (CSV)
docs.text:
Minimum 10 distinct failures. Use this exact header:

finding_id,category,what_you_gave_it,what_it_produced,why_wrong,severity,how_found,caught_by_test_suite

Allowed categories: syntax, invented-api, wrong-logic, insecure, memorised, prompt-sensitive, context-ignored, other. Severity: low / medium / high. For caught_by_test_suite, use yes / no.

docs.title: Appendix E: Improvement Report
docs.text:
• Target failure category and why you selected it.
  • Hypothesis (written before the run).
  • One change, described reproducibly.
  • Before/after comparison on the same probe set.
  • Compute cost, validation loss, and regressions.
  • Did the change work? Did it work for the reason you expected?
  • What would you try next?

docs.title: Appendix F: AI-Use Log
docs.text:
Date Tool What you asked What you accepted What you fixed How you verified

At the end, briefly reflect on: where AI helped, one confidently wrong result and how you caught it, whether AI reduced your understanding anywhere, and what you will do differently in Project 2.

docs.title: Appendix G: Handwritten AI-Literacy Reflection
docs.text:
Print this page and complete it by hand without AI assistance.

Topic Before (1–5) Now (1–5) How code becomes tokens and why tokenization matters What embeddings and self-attention do What next-token prediction / cross-entropy optimize Difference between training and inference How to read training vs. validation loss Why fluent output can still be wrong

Answer each question in 1–2 handwritten sentences:

  1. What can you explain now that you could not explain before this project?
  2. Did building and testing your own model change how you judge tools such as Copilot or ChatGPT? How?
  3. Which phase taught you the most, and why?
  4. What about language models still confuses you?

Optional: one change that would have helped you learn more from this project.
